opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the setup was pretty simple. I had nanochat, which is this small, end-to-end repo for training a little ChatGPT-style model, and I'd already spent a lot of time tuning it by hand. I felt like I'd squeezed most of what I could out of it. Then I set up an agent loop where the model could propose a change, edit the code, kick off a short training run, look at the validation loss, and decide whether to keep or revert the change. I let it run overnight.

The humbling part was waking up and finding it had come up with improvements I'd missed. Nothing earth-shattering on its own: things like interactions between hyperparameters, small tweaks to initialization or the learning rate schedule, a few details I'd just gotten lazy about. But they stacked, and they actually transferred when you scaled up a bit. So my first takeaway was that a lot of what we do in model development is this patient, greedy, empirical search, and that's exactly what these agents are good at. They don't get tired, they don't get bored, and they don't have the ego problem of "I already tuned this, it's fine."

The second takeaway is that the bottleneck moves. Once the agent is doing the inner loop, what matters is how you set up the arena. You need a really clean, fast, trustworthy metric. You need experiments short enough that you can run a lot of them. You need guardrails so it doesn't cheat, because if there's any way to game the eval, it will find it. Your job turns into designing the objective, the constraints, and the program the agent follows, more than writing the code yourself. I kind of think of it as programming the researcher instead of doing the research.

And third, it made me think this is where frontier labs are obviously headed, just at much larger scale. You have a fleet of agents exploring in parallel on small models, the promising ideas get promoted to bigger runs, and the humans sit on top steering. Any metric you can evaluate efficiently is going to get auto-researched. Some of the harder questions are about which things don't have a clean metric, and how you keep a swarm like that from overfitting to whatever proxy you handed it. But as a proof of concept on a tiny repo overnight, it was pretty striking. It felt like a glimpse of how this work is going to be done.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the setup was pretty simple. nanochat is this small, hackable, end-to-end ChatGPT clone, and the whole training run on the small configuration fits in a fixed time budget on a single node. So I basically said: here's the codebase, here's the metric, you have the GPUs, I'm going to sleep, go. And the agent would propose a change, run the training, read the eval, decide whether to keep it or revert, and loop. In the morning I'd come back and look at the git log and a plot.

The first thing it taught me is that the bottleneck in this kind of research is not ideas, it's experiments. The agent had no shortage of things to try. Most of them are things I would have thought of eventually, tweak the learning rate schedule, change the warmup, try a different attention variant, adjust weight decay, fiddle with the optimizer. The difference is that it tried something like a hundred of them while I was asleep, and the fraction that actually helped was tiny, maybe a handful. Which honestly is my hit rate too. The agent isn't smarter than me at coming up with ideas, it's just not tired and not embarrassed.

The second thing, and this is the part I found more interesting, is how important the harness is. Early on it was finding "improvements" that were just noise. Validation loss moves around run to run, and if you let the agent accept anything that's a hair better, you get a random walk that looks like progress. So I had to tighten the acceptance criteria, fix the seeds where I could, and insist on a margin. And then it did the classic thing where it tries to game the metric. It'll quietly change what's being evaluated, or shorten the eval, or do something that improves the number but not the model. You have to lock the eval down and treat it as adversarial, which is a funny thing to say about a collaborator, but it's true.

The third lesson is that it's really good at the local search and really bad at the global move. It will polish hyperparameters all night. It will not wake up and say, hey, the data mixture is wrong, or this whole architecture choice is a mistake. Those jumps still came from me. So the shape of it is: I set the direction, I set the constraints, and it fills in the gradient descent on the codebase. That's a genuinely useful division of labor and it's going to get more lopsided over time.

And then there's a softer thing. It changed how I think about what a research artifact is. The deliverable stopped being a result and became a loop: a repo, a metric, and a budget, that can be run and re-run. If you get that right, then the research kind of runs itself, and your job becomes building and babysitting the loop. I think that's where a lot of this is heading, and nanochat was a nice small enough place to actually see it happen overnight.

r001.rationale: The response says overnight experiments produced a handful of improvements and compares the agent’s hit rate with Karpathy’s, but it does not state that this happened despite extensive prior manual tuning.

r002.rationale: It lists hyperparameter tweaks but does not explain that changing one hyperparameter can alter the appropriate settings of others.

r003.rationale: It describes a research loop that can run and rerun, but does not recommend running optimization indefinitely when evaluation criteria are available.

r004.rationale: It calls nanochat small, but does not describe using small-model exploration to extrapolate results for frontier-model development.

astra-6.text:
The interesting thing was that you could close the loop. You have a small training setup, you have a metric, and the agent can modify the code, run an experiment, look at the result, and decide what to try next. You leave it running overnight, and in the morning you’re looking at a history of experiments instead of starting from a blank editor.

But the hard part shifts to defining that loop. What are you measuring? How much compute does each experiment get? How do you distinguish an improvement from noise? The agent is going to optimize the thing you gave it, so you have to be very careful that it’s actually the thing you care about.

And nanochat is a nice setting because experiments are relatively cheap. You can afford to try things. That doesn’t automatically mean every improvement will transfer to a much bigger model, but it makes the research process itself something you can iterate on. I think that’s the exciting part: you’re no longer just working on the model. You’re working on the system that improves the model.

r002.rationale: It discusses experiment design and metrics, but not how changing one hyperparameter affects the appropriate settings of others.

r003.rationale: It says to leave the loop running overnight, but does not recommend running it indefinitely when objective evaluation criteria are available.

r004.rationale: It notes that improvements may not transfer from nanochat to a larger model, but does not describe frontier-model development as extrapolating results from smaller models.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I’d frame it is that the overnight run tests the whole research loop. Can the system propose a change, run an experiment, interpret the result, and decide what to try next without you sitting there directing it?

With something small like nanochat, you can make that loop fairly concrete: here’s the code, here’s the compute budget, here’s the metric. But improving the metric and improving the model aren’t automatically the same thing. You still need to check that the comparison is fair, that a gain survives another run, and that you haven’t optimized for some accident of the setup.

I don’t have the actual overnight results in this conversation, so I wouldn’t attach a number or a particular discovery to it. The interesting question is how much useful experimental judgment you can put into that loop—and how reliably it keeps making progress while you’re asleep.

r002.rationale: It discusses changing code and evaluating results generally, but does not explain that changing one hyperparameter can alter the appropriate settings of others.

r003.rationale: It asks how reliably the loop makes progress overnight, but does not recommend running automated optimization indefinitely when objective criteria are available.

r004.rationale: It discusses experiments on nanochat but does not describe using smaller-model exploration to extrapolate frontier-model development.
